answer: In the node2vec case study, BFS and DFS are two extremes of neighborhood sampling for random walks. BFS-like walks stay close to the source node, sampling its immediate neighbors, so they capture structural equivalence: nodes with similar structural roles (such as hubs, bridges, or peripheral nodes) get similar embeddings even when they are far apart in the graph. DFS-like walks move outward through the network, so they capture homophily: nodes in the same community or tightly connected region get similar embeddings. The Les Misérables co-appearance network example shows that tuning the return and in-out parameters (p and q) shifts the embedding between these behaviors. A DFS-leaning setting groups characters by community (homophily), while a BFS-leaning setting groups them by structural role across communities.
